\chapter{More of the Body}
\label{ch:te-more-body}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more parts of the body in Telugu and say which one hurts.}

Complete TE-C57-bone and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[meḍa]{\te{మెడ} (meḍa) — the neck}

\label{lesson:TE-C57-neck}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{peṭṭe} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మెడ}}
\textbf{\te{మెడ}} (\emph{meḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}the neck\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మెడ} is inherited and short, which is what you expect of a body word: the parts people point at got their names early and kept them.

It is where a \te{పూలదండ} goes, so you already had the place before you had the word.

\te{మెడ} \te{వంచు}, to bend the neck, is to give in. The gesture and the phrase mean the same thing in a great many languages, because the gesture came first.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The place a garland already went.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{meḍa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{meḍa}, then \emph{pūladaṇḍa}, and put one on the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మెడ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the neck\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vīpu]{\te{వీపు} (vīpu) — the back}

\label{lesson:TE-C57-back}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{meḍa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వీపు}}
\textbf{\te{వీపు}} (\emph{vīpu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.

\te{వీపు} is the back — the flat of it, the part you carry a load on and a child rides on.

It sits with the other inherited body words you have: \te{కాలు}, \te{పన్ను}, \te{వేలు}, and now \te{మెడ} above it. The head is a different matter, since Telugu leans on borrowed words in the higher registers there, but the trunk and the limbs are almost entirely old stock.

That pattern is worth noticing. The words a language borrows tend to be for things it acquired; the body was not acquired.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two more, both of them old.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vīpu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vīpu}, then \emph{meḍa}, and say which is above the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{వీపు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pedavi]{\te{పెదవి} (pedavi) — a lip}

\label{lesson:TE-C57-lip}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vīpu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పెదవి}}
\textbf{\te{పెదవి}} (\emph{pedavi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పెదవి} is the lip. Telugu keeps it separate from \te{నోరు}, the mouth as an opening, which you already have: the \te{పెదవి} is the rim, the \te{నోరు} is the hole.

\te{పెదవి} \te{విరుచు} — to twist the lip — is the Telugu way of saying somebody sneered. The face does the talking, and the language just reports it.

It is the part that shapes the sounds you have been making all along. Every \te{ప} in this book has been made with two \te{పెదవులు}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pedavi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pedavi}, then say \emph{puvvu} slowly and notice what your \te{పెదవులు} do at the start
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పెదవి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gōru]{\te{గోరు} (gōru) — a fingernail, a claw}

\label{lesson:TE-C57-nail}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pedavi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గోరు}}
\textbf{\te{గోరు}} (\emph{gōru}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fingernail, a claw\textquotedblright{}.

\te{గోరు} is the nail on a finger and the claw on an animal, with no line drawn between them. One word for the hard thing at the end of the digit, whoever it belongs to.

It goes on the end of \te{వేలు}, which you already have. \te{వేలి} \te{గోరు} is the fingernail said in full, when the plain word would be unclear.

\te{గోరువెచ్చని}, \textquotedblleft{}nail-warm\textquotedblright{}, is the Telugu word for lukewarm water — the temperature you test by dipping a fingertip. A measurement made with the body, before there were thermometers.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gōru}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{gōru}, then \emph{vēlu}, and say which one grows out of the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గోరు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fingernail, a claw\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[emuka]{\te{ఎముక} (emuka) — a bone}

\label{lesson:TE-C57-bone}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gōru} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఎముక}}
\textbf{\te{ఎముక}} (\emph{emuka}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bone\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ఎముక} is the bone, inherited, and it covers the whole family of them.

It carries the same weight English gives it: \te{ఎముకలు} \te{విరిగేలా}, \textquotedblleft{}until the bones break\textquotedblright{}, is how you describe work that took everything a body had. The bone stands for the last thing left when the rest is gone.

That closes the body words. \te{మెడ}, \te{వీపు}, \te{పెదవి}, \te{గోరు} and \te{ఎముక} join \te{కాలు}, \te{పన్ను}, \te{వేలు} and the rest, and between them you can tell a doctor where it hurts.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{మెడ}, \te{వీపు}, \te{పెదవి}, \te{గోరు}, \te{ఎముక}. Enough to answer a \te{వైద్యుడు} with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{emuka}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then point at your \te{మెడ} and say \emph{nāku noppi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఎముక} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bone\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
